en: The Buddha-spoken Mahāvaipulya Śikhin-rāja Sūtra, also known as the Vimalakīrti-putra-paripṛcchā, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī Grove, together with a great [assembly].

Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus—eight hundred in number—and ten thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were great sages who had attained supernormal powers, had fully acquired dhāraṇīs, possessed unimpeded eloquence, and had mastered the wisdom of the three periods of time leading to the three types of transcendental knowledge; they did not realize the fruits of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness midway, but practiced great loving-kindness and offered boundless compassion, transcending to the other shore without reckoning a self.

He penetrates the three periods of time—past, future, and present—without attachment to them. He understands that all phenomena are like illusions, transformations, dreams, reflections, echoes, mirages, plantain trees, water bubbles, and masses of foam. He realizes that the three bases of perception are fundamentally non-existent, arising only through the conjunction of conditions. Whether facing gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or infamy, suffering or pleasure, he transcends all worldly dharmas. Through skillful means, he circulates within the three miserable realms to surpass the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

He elucidates the meaning of the Path to rescue and deliver all beings. When devas come to attend him, they inquire about and receive the profound Dharma; their deluded minds are awakened, and they all enter the light of the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for alms and arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti.

At that moment, Vimalakīrti had a son named Susīma, who had bathed in the morning and anointed his body with incense. Wearing new garments and holding a lotus flower in his hand, he ascended the upper terrace together with his wife to watch the performance of musicians and enjoy themselves—a manifestation of the karmic roots of virtue planted in past lives.

Seeing from afar the Buddha approaching with his assembly of noble ones entering the city for alms, he manifested a great auspicious transformation and addressed his wife in verse, singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues:
"Hearing this harmonious and elegant sound, produced by all at once, the many musicians in that place—
quickly ascend to the upper chambers of the pavilion!"
The Great Hero comes without doubt; the World-Protector radiates brilliant light.
He will surely tread upon the threshold of the city gate with his right toe.
The hundred birds and various beasts will raise their voices in mournful, harmonious song.
Never before in antiquity have such wondrous sounds been heard;
there is no doubt that the Great Hero has come, wishing to guide and benefit sentient beings.
Now he raises his right toe and places it upon the threshold of the gate.
Today I behold the Buddha, his body like a precious necklace;
though no music is played by the many maidens, it is subtle and delights the heart.
The Sage of the Three Thousand Worlds is free from doubt; his majestic virtue is pure and adorned.
He will surely step with his right toe upon the threshold of the city gate.
It is like a great bowl placed in a pool or river where the water rises to it;
then a harmonious sound is heard, pervading the entire land.
The Lord of Men, free from doubt, the Great Sage who radiates sublime light,
the Buddha who guides the world, will surely come through the city gates.
With supernatural powers he transforms sentient beings, like the flourishing blossoms of a tree.
Various colored flowers and blossoms spread an exquisite fragrance;
the Great Dragon, free from doubt, established his vow as the foundation.
Now, with the tip of his right foot, he places it upon the threshold of the city gate.
Universally illuminating the void, pervading heaven and earth,
the brilliance of the sun is eclipsed, and its light never appears again;
all Honored Ones are beyond doubt, manifesting majestic and great radiance.
Now, with the tip of his right foot, he placed it upon the threshold of the city gate;
just as the various devas abide in the midst of space,
the multitudes followed behind the Buddha, like the celestial hosts attending Brahmā.
Compassionately pitying the world without doubt, the Honored One, the Holy Teacher,
now places the tip of his right toe upon the threshold of the city gate.
Today, those who behold the city each turn toward one another with loving-kindness and harbor no resentment.
They conversed with one another in turn, like parents, children, and grandchildren;
his virtuous radiance was free from hesitation, and he was naturally adorned with the majesty of merit.
Now, with the tip of his right toe, he placed it upon the threshold of the city gate.
Observing men and women, great and small, each holding a certain number of flowers,
they joined their palms in self-refuge and joyfully scattered flowers from afar;
the Great Guide was free from hesitation, his body adorned with the flowers of virtue.
Now, with the tip of his right foot, he placed it upon the threshold of the city gate.
Flowers from among the devas and humans were spread throughout the void;
as flowers were scattered and incense burned, the fragrance brought delightful joy.
"The Great Hero, free from doubt and fetters, desires to enter Vaiśālī;
because he has transformed and gladdened the great assembly, this Most Victorious One has arrived here.

At that time, the wife of Sutasoma heard these words, and fear arose within her heart; the hair on her body stood on end and her inner being became chilled as she stood by the gate, thinking to herself:
"What kind of deity is this?
Is it a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a pādōna, a kinnara, a mahoraga, or a human or non-human being?"
He spoke with human speech.
Remaining in that place, he did not move, nor did he shake, nor did he dare to shift his position.
Then the Buddha went to the village where the youth Subuddhi resided and stood before the door at the side of the house.

When the youth Sudarśana saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he immediately wished to descend from the tower to go forth and welcome him. Overjoyed in his heart, unable to contain himself, he threw himself down from the tower to receive the Buddha’s holy command;
remaining suspended in mid-air, he praised the Buddha with these verses: “O Honored One of Noble Wisdom, please stay!
O Hero among Men, wait out of compassion, Out of pity for all sentient beings, Please accept this water and gruel.”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Sutasoma:
"Abiding in the true limit (bhūtakoṭi), which the worldly cannot fathom, That limit is non-existent;
such is the characteristic of the limit."
The youth Sudarśana questioned the Buddha in verse:
“How does one abide at the fundamental limit?
How is the true fundamental limit used to transform and guide? What is the limit of reliance upon ignorance? And what is meant by establishing in emptiness?”
Then the Buddha again addressed Suvicintin with these verses:
“That limit is the true ultimate limit; this limit is the Tathāgata.
If one dwells in the ultimate limit with thorough examination, one dwells clearly in suchness.”
"As the limit is the true original limit, so too is it the limit of the Tathāgata;
just as one thoroughly understands the true original limit, so too does the youth abide.
The youth Subhūti then addressed the Buddha again in verse:
"If there is no limit, what is the limit? What is the characteristic of that limit?
By what skillful means is it called the 'original limit'?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, perceiving that the mind of the youth Subhūti desired to fully comprehend that the Way has no fixed location, addressed the youth Subhūti with a verse, replying:
"Boundless and beyond expectation, it is called the true primordial limit;
its characteristic is like empty space, and even empty space has no characteristics.
Thus did Subhūti speak this verse to the Buddha and inquire:
"How profound is this state of true reality! That state is mysterious and unsurpassed;
may all sentient beings come to abide as they do now under this Teacher!
Then, the youth Subhūṣita came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accept these lotus flowers.
The Buddha then accepted them.
The youth Sudarśana spoke with his own mouth and body:
"By means of these merits, one shall attain the unexcelled, true, and correct path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment;
for the sake of all sentient beings, one shall proclaim the sūtras so that they do not fall into the ways of ordinary worldlings, nor do they remain fixed in the ways of the [limited] path."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also present in the assembly, and he said to the youth Subhūti:
"Subhūti, what is the direction of your mind?"
"What is the likeness of the Dharma of the Perfect Enlightenment you have attained?
You wish to proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus addressed, Suvicintin replied by reciting these verses:
“The Buddha’s resolve has nothing to be attained; the same is true for all śrāvakas.
One shall realize this perfect awakening and proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings.
That [awakening] has no destination toward which to speak, nor is there anything therein that can be pointed out.”
The one of great wisdom should understand this: that primordial purity and luminosity are thus.
The Tathāgatas of the past, the World-Protectors, the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, likewise did not apprehend any dharmas, yet they guided the world through their parinirvāṇa.
When one calculates and seeks, there is no realm of dharmas, nor is there a realm of sentient beings;
this is the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi), which is not fully expressed by worldly convention.
It is provisionally designated as a "world," for people rely upon characteristics and names.
"Furthermore, there are no conceptualizations, nor is there any other karma.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra spoke these verses for the sake of the youth Sudarśana:
"O youth, why do you wish to study this Dharma?"
This realm is profound and difficult to fathom, where even the wise are bewildered.
How long has it been since you, O Benevolent One, were born? Your wisdom alone is courageous and fierce;
when conversing with the śrāvakas, you respond instantly with fearless insight.
"Able to discern in every place, The images he dwells upon are like purple-gold;
He stands tall upon the royal road, Like the full moon in the void.
Then the youth Subhūṣita replied in verse:
“O Benevolent One, you ask about that which is born; yet that which is born is without birth.
Since all phenomena do not arise, who indeed could be born again?
These phenomena are without birth; by their very nature, they are non-existent.”
This is called primordial purity; there is no dharma and nothing to be attained.
All dharmas are primordially pure, yet none have ever been able to attain this.
Because of ignorance and pride, the Buddha has therefore taught this Dharma.
In the Wilderness of the Sages, he first turned this wheel;
there, the activities of the śrāvakas abound, and their resolve is fixed upon the void.
He proclaims the resonance of the Dharma-sound, acting as a source of manifold eloquence for the multitudes.
Using skillful means to bring forth noble wisdom, he proclaims it according to the ultimate truth:
that there is birth and then passing away; such ignorant conduct does not exist [in the enlightened], for they abide in inverted karma, as Pūrṇa has explained.
"Because birth exists, there is old age and death; this is the conventional expression of the world.
That Dharma is beyond words and speech; it is through relying on the provisional that verbal teachings are fashioned.
At that time, the worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is truly unprecedented, World-Honored One!
This youth Subhūti has now entered deeply into wisdom to such a sublime degree; that which he proclaims is peerless and beyond the reach of all others.”
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is!
It is exactly as Pūrṇa has spoken, without any difference."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattva, the youth Subhūti:
"For what reason do you wish to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path, and become a most perfectly awakened one?"
Suxi replied:

"It is because the Holy Honored One has clarified this that I ask you again; it is for the sake of the Great Sage that he has donned the great vow, and it is by virtue of the Great Sage’s supreme benevolence that these words have been proclaimed."

My body is tranquil and performs no action; because I am clothed in the great vow, there is nothing that obstructs me, and since there is nothing to be transformed or guided, this is what is called this profound and supreme phrase.
Sentient beings are likewise without a self; those who do not waver in this regard are able to deliver them.

The Most Worthy One has carefully set forth these profound, subtle, and supreme verses, clearly understanding this fundamental reality from beginning to end. Because they are innumerable and without distinction, they comprehend these profound, subtle, and unsurpassed chapters and phrases. By means of the Dharma, they transform these sentient beings; though their practices differ, in their teaching there are no sentient beings.

If there were no sentient beings, all would be empty; wisdom and the lack of wisdom are fundamentally pure in sentient beings. Because one realizes this fundamental purity, there is no distinction between them; to understand this meaning is the wisdom of the world.
“Indeed, O Holy One, having received this explanation, I shall attain perfect enlightenment for myself and preach the Dharma to the multitude.
Then the Venerable Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha:
“It is truly unprecedented! This youth Sudharma possesses such profound eloquence; he is able to proclaim these well-ordered, sublime verses and unattached phrases.”

When the common people of the heavens and the world, as well as the asuras, hear this, they will surely be terrified and refuse to accept its teachings; who then would believe in or delight in this profound and wondrous Dharma?
"In former lives, I once heard and studied this profound and far-reaching practice; only then did I come to believe and accept it.
At that time, Ānanda praised him in verse:
"Just like the summit of Mount Sumeru, It appears from afar, subtle and beautiful."
Now this one of virtuous reflection, amidst this assembly, is thus;
like the king of mountains firmly abiding in the great ocean,
he now stands within this multitude and joyfully proclaims these wondrous verses.
The well-considered praise you offer is called "neither being nor non-being";
it illuminates the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), which is not observed by worldly people.
Your words are fearless, and there is none who does not revere and admire them.
“Only you, Subhūti, speak of this: how is the beginning and the end known?
Subhūti replied in verse:
“I have cast aside my body and life, donning the armor of non-obstruction.”
When one’s resolve does not crave even perfect enlightenment, only then may one be called "widely learned.
Through attachment to desire, one falls; by amassing [evil], one incurs the utmost calamity.
Who would not fall into disaster, were it not for the World’s Guide?
This is the realm of all Buddhas, sustained and delivered by the World-Protectors;
their bodies are free from all affliction as they abide in the path of the Honored Buddha.
Both space and the human body are ultimately ungraspable.
Since phenomena are unattainable according to the Dharma, one harbors no fear regarding phenomena;
understanding that the Buddha-body is like space and truly has no location,
if one achieves such patience, one will forever be entirely without fear.
From the void down to the earth, there is naturally nothing at all;
this natural state of skillful reflection realizes that everything is without location.
From the void down to the earth, skillful reflection cannot be apprehended.
There is no arising and no spontaneity; it is empty, still, and devoid of anything existent.
Space has no height, nor does it have any depth.
By thoroughly understanding this Dharma, one is entirely without fear.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Subhūti:
"O worthy one, is your essential nature free from fear?
He replied to the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha asked him again:
"Are you truly not afraid?"
He replied, "No,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent!
You, O benevolent one, are fearless and harbor no dread.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Fear arises from existence; it is manifested as a mere conventionality of that which does not exist.
If one can understand this through patience, then one draws near to the Buddha-way.
Because of the conceptualization of persons, fear exists; yet sentient beings are fundamentally and eternally non-existent.”
If one can understand this thus, there is no abiding therein.
That which does not attain perfect awakening is likewise without awakening;
if there is nothing else to be gained, then perhaps there is nothing to fear.
"If one can clearly understand this and not abide in the extremes of existence or non-existence,
such skillful reflection and liberation is what constitutes following the Buddha-way.
The Buddha said to Suvicintin:

"If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to swiftly attain eternal peace and reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One, they should eliminate the notion of permanence, the notion of pleasure, the notion of suffering, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a person or a life-span; they should analytically understand and resolve upon practice free from attachment, remaining entirely without dependence."
By cultivating such meritorious deeds, one attains the realization of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

When the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path in past lives, he followed this way of cultivation; thus, he brought forth wisdom that cannot be grasped as a dharma, which is called the Buddha-way.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Understanding the notion of permanence as being like an illusion, One realizes that clinging to permanence leads to birth and death.
Both permanence and impermanence are empty and non-existent; Seeking karma, one finds it to be nothing at all."
Sentient beings harbor the notion of peace, yet they do not realize that non-peace is the natural state.
This notion is a perversion, arising because they conceive of a person.
If one understands phenomena, there are no distinct differences.
Thus, one harbors no expectations; there is no life and no person.
The Way is not attained through seeking, and the same holds true for non-Way.
This is called primordial purity, for phenomena possess nothingness.
If there are those who are clear-sighted and discerning, Who understand that all existence is fundamentally pure,
And who contemplate well to comprehend this— This is the true path of the Way.
Those who do not practice the vehicle of the Way Are rescued by the Buddha-vehicle.
If anyone disputes this, they shall not master the Dharma;
they do not practice the work of wisdom and are not protected by the Way.
Because they do not accord with this conduct, the Buddha-dharma is profound and difficult to understand.
All phenomena are devoid of inherent nature; fundamentally, they are all without form or appearance.
All that exists is likewise empty and non-existent; the three realms are forever without peace.
To reckon all pleasures as manifold sufferings is like traveling through empty space.
If one can contemplate this practice, the mind is thereby liberated.
That which possesses a body is called "self," yet those phenomena are likewise empty and non-existent.
Since there is no self, that which is known is nothing at all.
These people do not contemplate life; they cannot investigate its beginning or end.
They take the void for reality, and their slight clarity is but delusion.
The self and the life-span are fundamentally pure and non-existent.
The conduct of the ignorant and deluded is to calculate that there is existence based on primordial purity;
yet the Buddha-way is inconceivable, and they do not contemplate that all these things exist.
If they hear the profound and wondrous Dharma, they are unable to receive and uphold it.
Never before has there been one who proclaims such a sutra and dharma;
the Dharma cannot be grasped, and that which is spoken is likewise unattainable.
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he thereby attained the wisdom of the Way.
If one does not attain the wisdom of the Path, then there is likewise nothing to be known.
The Buddha-way and the field of wisdom are beyond verbal expression;
yet ordinary people harbor expectations and long for the Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha.
This is the true teaching, the profound and subtle proclaimed by the Buddha;
its meaning is most deep, yet it is that which Māra practices.
If there are those who hear this sūtra spoken by the Buddha,
Not understanding the flavor of the meaning of the sūtras, nor that which all dharmas protect and preserve;
the bodhisattva undergoes great hardship yet does not seek the peace and security of the Way;
in this, there is no awakening to the Way—these two matters are without form.
The mind should rely upon and aspire to this; this is what the Buddha has taught.
What is this? How is it? It is attachment to inverted karma;
if there is the suffering of transgression, one is deeply attached to that which is profound and subtle.
Each raised their voices in great resonance, exclaiming, "We rejoice in the Buddha’s inconceivable [wisdom]!
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:

"Those who study this Dharma should practice the profound scriptures; they must not set their minds on miscellaneous phrases, flowery rhetoric, or meaningless doctrines, for these will not bring about the true, correct, and infinite great wisdom."
The profound and far-reaching Dharma is called sublime and vast; that which accords with this Dharma is called non-attainment.
Sentient beings fall into error and are unable to practice this; it cannot be understood through the benefits of worldly samādhis.
Wisdom has no objective realm, and the same is true for non-wisdom; one should understand that this limit is not within the sphere of intellectual activity.
In past lives, the Buddha heard this profound Dharma and, through understanding its tranquil purity, his mind was free from all attachment.

If one hears this scripture and attains joy and gladness, it is because they have, in the presence of countless Buddhas, cultivated practices and established meritorious virtues; having received and cherished it in their hearts, they recite and practice it, transforming others and proclaiming it throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha again addressed the youth Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva should cultivate such a great vow. While worldly people everywhere are constantly gripped by fear, one who diligently studies the Ultimate Truth should not harbor any dread.
When encountering difficulties that cause one to retreat, one should understand them in this way; by proclaiming and practicing [the Dharma], one enters the wisdom of the Path."
Sushīla came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, I have faith and joy. That which the world does not believe, I alone hold with unending devotion; my will is as vast as space, forever free from longing."
The Buddha spoke again to Suvicintin:

"If a bodhisattva mahāsattva is resolved upon the profound and wondrous Dharma, these true persons (satpuruṣa), by means of such skillful means, will accord with the Buddha's teaching; they will not engage in dispute regarding the dharmas of the Path. Because they do not dispute, they shall have no fear regarding any dharmas, and none of them are to be severed.
Realizing that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, their resolve becomes free from longing, and they thereby enter the wisdom of the Path."
If one hears it said that all phenomena exist, one does not become afraid;
if it is said that they do not exist, one does not become anxious.
Regarding existence and non-existence, one does not increase or diminish one's hearing [of the Dharma].
All dharmas are appropriate; all dharmas are inappropriate; all dharmas are diligence; all dharmas are indolence.
To understand all these dharmas of the ten directions is that to which wisdom returns.
If there is no destination, or if one does not understand whether all phenomena possess mindfulness or are devoid of mindfulness, one does not become terrified;
whether all phenomena are conditioned or unconditioned, whether all phenomena have boundaries or are boundaryless, whether all phenomena are joyful or joyless, one does not become terrified;

all phenomena are neither conditioned nor unconditioned, all phenomena are originally existent and originally non-existent, whether all phenomena are tranquil or turbulent, one does not become terrified.
All dharmas are inverted or non-inverted; all dharmas are void and non-existent, yet truly unconditioned—without being terrified by this.

All dharmas possess precepts or lack precepts, clarity or ignorance, names or namelessness, arising or non-arising, fear or fearlessness, birth or non-birth, death or non-death—without being terrified by these.
All dharmas have the Path or no Path; all dharmas have liberation or non-extinction; all dharmas are right or wrong—without being terrified by these.
Why is this? All dharmas are empty, void, and unreal, like illusions, transformations, bubbles, foam, plantain trees, shadows, echoes, and mirages;
they are like what is seen in a dream, fundamentally having no place from which they come and no place to which they go.

It is like space, where clouds, mist, dust, smoke, or ashes may suddenly appear; though these manifest within space, they cannot defile it, and when they suddenly vanish, space itself remains naturally without anything to be purified.
Whether there is the Way or not the Way, one possesses worldly wisdom and clarity; universally understanding that all things are spontaneous, one then remains unattached.
Realizing there is nothing to be realized, one accords with the supreme, true, and correct wisdom of the Way, free from all fear and without harboring any anxiety in the mind.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are non-existent; They are naturally empty and not real.
That which is naturally empty and non-existent— This very characteristic is nirvāṇa."
All dharmas are without contention, and these too are non-existent;
by realizing that all dharmas are non-existent, one penetrates their natural non-existence.
Those dharmas that are subjects of dispute are likewise non-existent.
By understanding that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, one is liberated from contention and dispute.
All dharmas are without possession; they are fundamentally pure and eternally formless.
This fundamental purity is ungraspable, and there is likewise nothing to be lost.
Severing all phenomena, one is therefore called wise;
this is what is meant by eternal destruction, yet it is also manifested as having nothing to destroy.
All phenomena are not subject to extinction, and they are reckoned to have no arising or establishment.
Furthermore, for the most part, there is nothing to be destroyed, and dharmas are likewise unattainable.
All dharmas are fundamentally empty and non-existent, and they cannot be perceived;
yet even though they are unobtainable, they are manifested through skillful means.
All phenomena are non-existent, arising from conditions through mutual opposition;
whether existent or non-existent, they are proclaimed within the scriptures.
All phenomena are capable of harmonizing, manifesting a state free from contention.
Non-contention is the natural state; ultimately, there is no form.
All phenomena have nothing to which they correspond; they are without action and do not pass into extinction.
Thus, they cannot be apprehended, for they are eternally free from all numerical categories.
All phenomena are unattainable, and there is nothing past; how profound!
They are eternally without reality, and thus are called the primordial limit of truth (*bhūtakoṭi*).
All phenomena are joyful, yet they cannot be rejoiced in.
If phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are likewise beyond verbal expression.
All phenomena are without negligence; both are non-existent.
Naturally there is nothing to be grasped—this is the mark of the profound and wondrous.
All phenomena are unknowable; they are selfless and spontaneous.
Through understanding that there is nothing to be sought, one arrives at the state called spontaneity.
Being unconditioned, there is no delight therein, for even that is non-existent.
Because there is the karma of ignorance, it is designated as "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta).
If one contemplates all phenomena and finds they are ultimately invisible, this is a true statement;
therefore, it is called "mental attention" (manasikāra).
Not dwelling on any phenomena, Without abiding and without a place of return, Thoroughly understanding that there are no sentient beings— This is called the Dharma within the Dharma.
All phenomena are like illusions; Yet those illusions have no inherent existence.
Because of ignorance regarding phenomena, one speaks of birth and death.
All phenomena are without form or appearance; this is their natural meaning.
If there were no phenomena, there would be neither liberation nor non-liberation.
"Conventionally designated as 'realms,' they are naturally without realms;
because the ignorant and deluded rely upon and cling to them, they are called 'sectarian boundaries.
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:
"Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty and fundamentally non-existent;
the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty and fundamentally non-existent;
earth, water, fire, and wind are empty and likewise formless."
The combination of causes and conditions is like five things coming together to form a house.
What are these five? First is timber;
second is tiles and thatch; third is the earthen foundation; fourth is human labor; and fifth is mortar and water. It is through these five things that a house is completed.
Originally, at each distinct moment, there was no such thing as a "house.
It is through the combination of causes and conditions that it comes to be; the body is likewise so.
When the five aggregates encounter their respective conditions, the four great elements arise, and by virtue of this designation, it is called a "body."

Earth, water, fire, and wind each come together through conditions; it is like the four pillars and four walls of a house, all meeting through causes and conditions. Their formation and their disintegration both have no fixed location.

It is just as if one were to see in a dream houses, cities, trees with flowers and fruit, flowing waters, fields, plows, oxen, and various seeds; one sows the five grains, which each grow according to the season, and the master of the household, applying his mind, harvests them for his own sustenance.

The mind and spirit are shrouded in ignorance and fail to realize that all three realms are empty; because they rely on and long for objects, consciousness arises, and through the twelve links of dependent origination, beings wander and circulate back and forth. Thus they revolve without end, exhausting their mental faculties as they sink into the five destinies without a moment’s respite.
Not understanding that the fundamental nature is empty like what is seen in a dream, one awakens to find no place of origin and no destination toward which to turn.
Only upon attaining perfect enlightenment does one realize that the five destinies fundamentally have no location, and thus walk alone without fear.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Form, sensation, perception, and consciousness are empty; The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and mind are fundamentally quiescent and non-existent;
Earth, water, fire, and wind are distinct [from them].”
Having realized the realms, they attain mastery; they proclaim the teachings without fixed sections or chapters.
What they speak of as superior Buddha-lands is but the perception of nirvana within their own spheres.
All phenomena have their respective forms, yet fundamentally there is no coming together.
Not understanding emptiness and stillness, one does not realize that its essence is originally without a body;
there is nothing to be attained and nothing to be reached, for it is formed through the convergence of conditions;
there is nothing to be acquired and nothing to be brought forth, yet again, the hope for attainment arises.
In that state, one does not cultivate precepts, nor does one transgress prohibitions;
there is neither practice nor precepts—this is the characteristic of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
All phenomena are non-existent, arising from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there is the dharma of ignorance, one then creates the wisdom of clear penetration.
All dharmas have only provisional names; these are called "non-existent.
When provisional designations lack any real dharma, that is what is termed "nirvana."
That which arises has no place of birth; though the five aggregates appear due to causes, those aggregates are not to be seen, yet they are designated as appearing due to causes.
All that exists has no fixed location; it is through transformation that causes manifest as existing phenomena.
The Dharma is free from the karma of birth and death, And forever lacks the perils of birth and death.
Like a magician conjuring forms, The ignorant and deluded claim there are people;
Yet what exists is non-existent— The wise are not deluded by this.
Phenomena arise from that which has no arising; the wise hold no such reckoning.
All phenomena are entirely empty, yet the foolish do not understand this.
When a phenomenon has arisen, it must then come to an end.
Regarding birth, aging, and death, one who abandons them has nothing to fear.
All phenomena are entirely empty; even phenomena have no place of return.
One should contemplate this well and understand it—this is the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
Perfect Awakening is without action, and thus it is unattainable;
if one does not grasp at a locus for the Way, then one perceives the phenomena of the triple world.
If one harbors conceptual expectations regarding the Buddha-way, then one does not seek perfect awakening.
If one’s practice and resolve are set upon the Way, one will never again create the state of non-conception.

All births and deaths are spontaneous; yet if one does not contemplate these spontaneous phenomena, and realizes that spontaneity itself is non-existent, this is what is meant by the "conception of the unconditioned."
Ultimately there is nothing that arises; what is taught cannot be apprehended.
Because one practices the karma of ignorance, one thereby demonstrates the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
By harboring and bringing forth manifold meanings, all dharmas are then spontaneously so.
Since all those things are utterly unarisen, there is no matter for dispute;
since there is nothing they do not practice, they proclaim the profound and wondrous Dharma.
For the sake of arising for the benefit of all, the Bodhisattva practices compassion.
At that time, Subhūti (Suxi) replied to the World-Honored One in verse:
“The Buddha has appeared in the world, Out of compassion for us all;
For those whose bodies are ensnared by doubt, He proclaims this meaning of the Dharma.”
The Buddha’s emergence is inconceivable; he manifests a full array of transformations to destroy Māra’s net and preach the elimination of the sixty-two views.
Having severed the root of birth and death, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree.
Forever free from hesitation, he proclaims the elimination of all conceptual attachments;
having clarified the nature of deceptive karma, the Capable One extinguishes all views.
Acting with valor for the sake of the world, he cuts through my many doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Subhūti: "The conduct of a bodhisattva is never false; it provides great protection and succor through acts of grace.

It is free from contention and dispute, having removed all blemishes and being entirely without defilement. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he practices profound and far-reaching principles, harboring no expectations. Seeing that the world lacks solidity, he eliminates greed and desire; through this absence of greed, he casts off all fetters. He constantly maintains a mind of equanimity toward all beings, his resolve never being false. In the practice of great kindness, phenomena are ungraspable; he cultivates the roar of the Great Meaning without abandoning diligence. His mental activity reaches the ultimate truth and he does not lose his industrious efforts. Free from harm, he practices patience and does not engage in disputes. Having nothing to perceive, he honors the sublime practice day and night."

With right reflection and single-mindedness, abandon indolence and accomplish the practice of the Path. With a concentrated mind in meditative absorption, his heart is tranquil; he cultivates sublime wisdom, and regarding all dharmas, he ultimately finds nothing to be grasped. He acts with fearlessness, his mind neither cowed nor weak; he manifests the Bodhi-mind and practices without obstruction. Having accomplished the ten powers of a Tathāgata, by what conduct shall he proceed toward extraordinary deeds? Honoring that supreme wisdom which is peerless, he wanders through the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, practicing without hindrance to deliver and liberate all beings.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Practicing deeds free from falsehood—this is the speech of all Bodhisattvas.
By honoring the gates of liberation, they do not fear any obstructing actions."
Non-action is called right action; this is the work of a bodhisattva.
If one can understand this practice, there will be nothing to crave or seek.
To rescue and gather others through the Dharma—this is what all bodhisattvas proclaim.
The meaning of non-attainment is the practice that is unsurpassed.
To say, "I practice the Dharma," is to abide in perversion;
by abiding in perverted karma, one then incurs fear.
Should there be disputes and litigation, if one does not perceive where the dispute resides, the wise person attains such realization and practices the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
This vehicle is fearless; the Great Vehicle is most supreme.
Fear and fearlessness—these too are without negligence;
all things are non-existent, the most supreme among all practices.
If one realizes that all is empty and still, they shall practice the unsurpassed path.
This practice is most subtle and wondrous, protecting and rescuing all dharmas;
its salvation is profound and far-reaching, eliminating all expectations and conceptualizations.
Its conduct is remote and mysterious, for both [subject and object] have no fixed location.
If one can know the ultimate limit, one does not rely on thoughts regarding phenomena.
Phenomena are eternally free from all defilements, yet they do not depart by being separated from them;
these phenomena are fundamentally pure, and thus one should instead proclaim the relinquishing of desire.
Yet they manifest perverse rebellion, showing that desire is not solid;
without turning back from the work of words, these phrases are unsurpassed.
Unattached like a phantom, this is indeed beyond verbal instruction.
By abandoning perverse conduct, one is free from the intent for dispute;
the conduct of all sentient beings is ultimately unattainable.
If one can clearly understand this, such conduct is indeed the sublime teaching.
Sentient beings, because of ignorance, are called "the masses";
the nature of sentient beings is likewise so—this path is unsurpassed.
To contemplate sentient beings is to find that they are forever ungraspable.
This is the first [form of] loving-kindness; its praise is indeed infinite.
This is called the great gift of the world; this is what constitutes a Great Being (mahāsattva).
Always longing for and delighting in relinquishment—this is called the mind of the path of wisdom.
Even if one does not attain the Dharma, knowing that all phenomena are empty and without reality,
yet being clear and penetrating as a bodhisattva— this is called excelling in giving.
Understanding that phenomena cannot be attained, one is then free from all fear.
When there is no dharma to be honored, it is called giving;
when the form of dharmas cannot be grasped and the Buddha-dharma is inconceivable,
this is the precept of non-transgression, wherein all dharmas are without attachment.
The Buddha-fields are inconceivable; herein one does not perceive any realms.
Not harboring expectations regarding the precepts, this is what all Bodhisattvas praise.
Being able to endure all sentient beings, yet realizing that nothing whatsoever can be apprehended—this is the path.
"The instruction and admonition of the Buddha is that this Dharma is the foremost patience.
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:
"Form is empty and cannot be apprehended; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also empty and cannot be apprehended."

That which is called emptiness: form is itself emptiness, and there is no emptiness other than form; sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, and there is no emptiness other than them. The four great elements, the five aggregates, the eighteen constituents, and the three realms are fundamentally empty; the twelve links of dependent origination are empty by their very absence, and there is no emptiness other than them.
The mundane world and the supramundane, the conditioned and the unconditioned—all four great elements are empty, and there is no emptiness other than this.

Form is like a mass of foam; sensation is like a bubble; perception is like a plantain tree; volitional formations are like a dream; consciousness is like an illusion. The three realms are like transformations, and the five destinies are like shadows. They are like shadows because they arise from the encounter of conditions.

The three realms—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—are fundamentally and ultimately products of the mind and its volitions; they are like a painter preparing a plain wall or wooden panel, which are then brought into being through the convergence of causes and conditions.
Just as a flying bird traverses the air, so too does the Bodhisattva travel through the ten directions without harboring expectations or attachments;
just as the sun’s palace moves through space without defiling the various darknesses, so too does the Bodhisattva walk alone through the triple world with a mind free from clinging.

Having dispelled the profound obscurity of the three poisons—lust, anger, and ignorance—the Bodhisattva is like a lotus born from the mud yet remaining untainted by it. Likewise, while dwelling within birth and death, the Bodhisattva attains supreme perfect enlightenment; his mind is pure as space, forever free from attachment as he delivers all beings.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"When the mind cannot be apprehended, there is no contention;
if sentient beings cannot be apprehended, this is the foremost forbearance."
The Bodhisattva is free from indolence;
his resolve has no [worldly] activity, and he never exerts himself in cultivation. This is called the most supreme diligence.
His body and mind are sent forth directly and without deviation.
The Bodhisattva has nothing to say; this is the foremost diligence.
If there are those who are indolent, the Bodhisattva transforms and establishes them.
Being without mind and without activity, he abides in the foremost diligence.
That mind cannot be apprehended; it is without attachment internally or externally.
If the mind cannot be grasped, this is what constitutes a concentrated mind.
When the mind is constantly and diligently cultivated, it naturally becomes non-existent.
Without thought and without meditative attainment, one is said to have reached samādhi;
thus it is called "concentrated mind. Because one can perform such practice, abiding in this state is called "spontaneity," and this is the foremost concentrated mind.
Not knowing where wisdom resides, what dharma is it that is spontaneous?
Both spontaneity and wisdom are utterly non-existent;
this dharma cannot be apprehended, for such consciousness practices the true Dharma.
One does not cognize phenomena through consciousness; they are naturally non-existent.
If one realizes this practice, the Bodhisattva’s resolve becomes firm and strong;
practicing the supreme meaning, there is no destination in the world.
“The assembly is peerless; for the sake of the multitude, he proclaims the Dharma.
Although these beings dwell and travel about, they harbor no conceptual notions of sentient beings.
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:

"All dharmas are like illusions; these illusions are fundamentally empty and non-existent. It is because the deluded and ignorant common folk falsely reckon themselves and others as having substantial existence that they sink into the five destinies. One who is able to clearly understand that all these are non-existent has nothing to fear.
Since all dharmas have no beginning or end and possess neither interior nor exterior, one who understands them thus will have no timidity in mind."

The three realms are not difficult to transcend, for the three realms are entirely empty. If there is a bodhisattva who understands that these are fundamentally non-existent, they can walk alone through the three periods of time without difficulty. They penetrate birth and death as being like empty space; it has no form and is fundamentally nameless, and all dharmas are likewise without form and without name.

Due to ignorance, one races through the three realms, revolving without end; yet it is like the five elements abiding in space, which cannot be defiled. Because it is spontaneous, the mind is fundamentally pure;

because of provisional conditions, it is not immediately liberated, and thus the three poisons arise. Obscured by the guest-dust of the five aggregates and six decays, although there is right and wrong, these do not defile the fundamental purity. When the mind is universally open and penetrating, and the emptiness of the three periods of time is fully realized, one enters the Great Way.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Sentient beings are like illusions; these illusions have no inherent existence.
For one who proclaims such a truth, there shall forever be nothing further to fear."
Both oneself and others are equally empty and quiescent;
by being able to understand this, one will forever be without fear.
Regarding internal and external phenomena, do not calculate that they exist anywhere.
Do not harbor a timid or weak mind, nor find difficulty in the mundane world.
All phenomena are without obstruction, like revolving through empty space;
wherever they go, they are like empty space—such is the nature of these phenomena.
If one can understand this, the Bodhisattva has nothing to fear;
they discern all phenomena and comprehend the conduct of sentient beings.
Yet they do not apprehend a "sentient being," for all such phenomena are exactly like this.
By analyzing all realms, one finds that these realms do not exist;
this is called entering the practice of the Way, and this is called the unsurpassed Way.
To achieve this supreme deed, one comes to know the mental activities of sentient beings.
The various elements and sentient beings—both are non-existent;
by contemplating them thus, one fully understands all phenomena.
Regarding internal and external matters, there is no association, expectation, or conceptualization.
To think that by not abandoning phenomena, one reaches what is called the true limit (bhūtakoṭi)—
this dharma is inconceivable, and thus it is called the Buddha-dharma;
yet all these are non-existent, and none of them are established.
When one's practice can be thus, and when one reckons that no person exists,
then through the wisdom of non-action, it is called the Buddha-wisdom.
This vehicle is the Great Vehicle, which brings universal peace to all.
Never fearing this world, for the world has no inherent existence;
though dwelling within the world and throughout all realms of existence,
the Bodhisattva has no fixed abode as they seek unsurpassed wisdom.
This Dharma is profound and far-reaching; the Buddha-Dharma is inconceivable.
If there is no dharma to be attained, then one is close to the path of the Buddha.
As for that Buddha and his sutra-Dharma, all these are entirely non-existent.
If one practices in this way, one shall draw near to the Buddha-way.
Because one practices in this way, no worldly person can be their peer;
with a mind free from attachment, they indeed draw near to the Buddha-way.
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:

“If there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, upon hearing this profound sutra, read, uphold, recite, and chant it with hearts free from fear, and who are well-armed with the heart of great vows as adamantine, they will swiftly approach the Bodhi tree and sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). They will draw near to the realm of the Buddhas and attain personal realization of the True Suchness (*tathatā*), the unimpeded gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), and the contemplation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) which is beyond all conjunction. Reaching the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions, they will establish and practice great compassion and the boundless path of pity. They will perfect the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); their wisdom, most honored throughout the three periods of time, is like the sun and moon; their virtue has no equal, and their wisdom surpasses empty space. Their radiance of the Way is so sublime it cannot be compared, and they shall attain the boundless, holy mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*).”
If there are those who hear this infinite and sublime dharma and, having proclaimed this profound sūtra for others, believe in and delight in it, they must have seen countless Buddhas in past lives.

Furthermore, regarding those who do not treat it with disrespect or engage in derisive laughter: the Buddha, having foreseen and observed the person's fundamental nature, has long perceived their early faith in this sutra.

If one does not believe in, delight in, or practice this scripture, but instead treats hearing it with mockery, such a person is merely an outsider of heterodox teachings, a member of the retinues of various Māras, or a person of negligence.
Those who believe in this Dharma are disciples of the Buddha; the Buddha is their teacher and kinsman, through whom they achieve fulfillment, shave their hair and beards, and become śramaṇas.
Those who do not believe are of external, heterodox practices—the ninety-six kinds that act in opposition to the Way and the Dharma.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Seeing the Buddha seated beneath the tree, Practicing the true site of enlightenment—
Those who do not believe in the Buddha-way Cannot attain this wisdom."
That dharma which is without obstruction is ultimately unattainable;
realizing that dharmas have no location—this is called liberation.
When the mind enters noble wisdom, it becomes the sovereign of all dharmas.
All phenomena and the wisdom of the path are not what the Buddha has proclaimed.
Conditioned and unconditioned states are the objects of hope and imagination conceived by the ignorant;
for all Bodhisattvas there is no such conceptualization, for the Buddhas are the Great Sages of Supreme Clarity.
Observing this world universally, the world is entirely unfindable;
that by which one understands the world likewise has no location.
Regarding the Buddha, the sages, and sentient beings, therein is no expectation or conceptualization.
That which is without conceptual thought— how excellent is this unsurpassed compassion!
Even if the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm were likewise so,
this is what is called the bodhisattva’s non-attachment.
Because one perceives sorrow, yet that sorrow has no form or appearance;
since that sorrow is without appearance, it is not something the ignorant can comprehend.
Five things abide in space; they neither exist nor have a location.
All worldly things are thus; this is indeed unsurpassed compassion.
That unsurpassed True Dharma is called the Buddha-Dharma;
this world of non-attachment is the Dharma of Nature.
That which is illumined by the World-Protectors has no color whatsoever;
because it is a formless dharma, it is called "the invisible crown.
Like space, it is without limit; universally level, it cannot be grasped.
This is the True Dharma of the Buddha, Named "The Unobservable.
Its wisdom cannot be attained; It is the unsurpassed Great Way.
Since this wisdom cannot be grasped, Therein is nothing that is solid or permanent.
This shore and the other shore—what is seen is as if not seen;
one who deeply understands does not practice this, for it is sought through false conceptualization.
Mindfulness is the dharma of wisdom; this dharma is then equanimous.
One who violates this teaching of the Buddha is not a virtuous friend;
one who lacks diligence, or who practices with misplaced diligence, has reached a state of falsehood;
and one who does not practice with equanimity is not a virtuous friend.
Those bhikṣus who give rise to these dharmas, or again, those who cause these dharmas to cease,
do not properly contemplate the Buddha’s teaching;
for they are able to sever all suffering, which is fundamentally pure and non-existent.
"One who expounds the Dharma in this manner shall propagate the Buddha's teachings.
The Buddha further addressed Suvicintin:

"If one says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise from habituation, it is because of the habituation of the three realms that one cultivates the path; because of the conceit of a self (*ātman*), one practices great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) and cultivates immeasurable pity (*karuṇā*); relying upon the three realms, one practices the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); out of regard for the four great elements, one practices impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self (*anātman*); by means of birth, old age, sickness, and death, one seeks the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); by means of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one masters the twelve divisions of the scriptures; by means of the eighteen modes of conduct, one practices the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*); because the multitudes of the ten directions commit the ten evils, one practices the ten virtues and seeks the ten powers (*bala*); because of the three corruptions, one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*); because of attachment to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), one practices the six perfections (*pāramitā*). Walking alone with the six supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), one administers medicine according to the illness to rescue those in peril and distress."

The Buddha is like a skilled physician and the sutras and dharmas are like medicine; it is because of illness that there is a physician and medicine, yet when one is without illness, there is no medicine. All things are fundamentally empty—without form, without name, and even without provisional designations. The mind is equal to space, peerless and without companion; suddenly boundless, one then accords with the Way.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Dharma that has no abiding place— To practice therein, to proclaim it,
and to cultivate its elimination, Is to remain very far indeed from the Buddha-Dharma.”
If one forms false conceptualizations regarding this quiescent Dharma,
then by means of these false dharmas, one does not draw near to nirvāṇa.
To proclaim contention as being nirvāṇa— this is [the error].
One of good reflection should understand this: there is no practice of right view herein;
if one practices the Path while proclaiming rebellious acts, and if friends are disorderly and perverted—this is the work of a student.
The Buddha’s discourses and teachings, expounded by the Bodhisattva of great renown, are for the sake of those who will study them in the future; therefore, he exhorts them to practice the Path.
If there are those who uphold these profound and wondrous transformations of the Buddha, [they shall attain liberation].
Using all sentient beings as offerings to the Buddha;
if there are those of clear wisdom who receive and uphold this true Dharma,
such individuals will, in future ages, abide by means of the True Dharma.
"Those who do not practice this Dharma, whose minds remain established in conceptual thought, and who claim for themselves that they correspond to wisdom, will not attain the Way by other means.

When the Buddha preached this sutra, the youth Subhāṣita immediately attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Overjoyed and filled with delight, he leaped into the air to a height of four zhang and nine chi above the ground.

At that time, the Buddha smiled with joy; five-colored light, magnificent and most wondrous—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and purple—issued from his mouth, illuminating immeasurable Buddha-lands in the ten directions. It returned to circle the Buddha three times before entering through the crown of his head. This great trichiliocosm shook in six ways. In the void above, the heavens rained down finely pounded sandalwood incense and various fragrances such as *mukhā* (wood-milk); they rained down exquisite celestial flowers so brilliant they dazzled the eyes. Lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck, adorning the void and surrounding the ten directions so that there was nowhere not embellished.

In this trichiliocosm, various jewels were arrayed in exquisite and marvelous lattices; there were wondrous canopies, lofty pavilions, trees, flowing streams, and bathing ponds, from which the five musical tones issued together—harmonious, elegant, and plaintive. Upon hearing or seeing these transformations, there was no one who did not rejoice, feeling as though they had attained what they had never experienced before.
The worthy Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason do you smile?"
"Since you smile, there must be a purpose.
He then praised the Buddha with a verse:
"The Holy Honored One never speaks falsely; The Great Illumination does not rejoice in vain."
The Hero of the World, out of compassion, has spoken; for what reason do you smile?
Abiding in the midst of the void, the gods make offerings to the Supreme among Men, each singing praises with their own mouths:
"How wonderful is the proclamation of the Sūtras!"
Like a high lamp or a flash of lightning, with various subtle colors, such brilliance is likewise; its light shines both far and near.
Like the Dharma of all Buddhas, it bestows the definitive decision of the Right Path.
Circling the body three times, it suddenly vanished into the crown of the head;
the Holy Honored One’s smile shone with brilliance, and various kinds of light-colored rays issued from the Buddha’s mouth and entered his crown—
pray, speak of the meaning of this auspicious omen.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for the sake of the Venerable Ānanda:
“O son of noble family, Subhūti, you have established immeasurable merit;
you shall attain the awakening of a Tathāgata and reach the state of a Honored One among gods and humans.”
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“This youth Sudarśana shall encounter incalculable hundreds of billions of nayutas of Buddhas. In every lifetime he will follow and attend them, never being far from them, and he will always serve those Buddhas with a sincere heart, providing robes, food and drink, bedding and furniture, and medicines for the sick.

After the Buddhas have passed into parinirvāṇa, he will make offerings to their śarīras, erecting many jeweled stūpas forty thousand *li* high; placing the śarīras within these jeweled stūpas, he will honor and serve them with exquisite incense, various flowers, garments, diverse and wonderful jewels, music, banners, and streamers, as well as sandalwood and blended perfumes, liberation-flowers, and various silken fabrics, using these to serve all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.”

In the final age at the end of time, he shall attain the Way of the Buddha, receiving the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat, known as Vimalaprabha.
At that time, the Great Sage spoke in verse:
"If one were to fill the realms of the ten directions with various kinds of jewels and offer them as a gift to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas who protect the world;
"If one hears this sutra, their merit shall exceed that of such giving;
abiding in power, they preach the Dharma, protecting the world and illuminating the three realms.

At that time, Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, was filled with joy and delight, experiencing something unprecedented. He reflected that the Buddha’s supreme holiness surpassed Mount Sumeru, his wisdom transcended the three periods of time, and his Way was incomparable—like space, it has no peer. He probes the past and knows the present, his vision is boundless; his intelligence is luminous and vast, beyond all metaphor. His salvation from calamity and universal illumination are like the infinite void, as all beings receive his compassion.
At that time, Śāriputra, mindful of the Buddha’s kindness and virtue, spoke with reverence and recited these verses in praise:
“This sutra is most subtle and wondrous, Proclaimed by the Protector of the World;
Yet its name has not been spoken— How can one know its title?”
Never heard before in antiquity, this Dharma is now proclaimed;
having no place of abiding, how marvelous is the joy of preaching this Dharma!
Whether it be tainted phenomena or untainted phenomena—
In calculation, there is likewise nothing to be attained; how marvelous is this excellent teaching of the Dharma!

If one were to cause both the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) and the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) to have no accumulation whatsoever, this sutra would accord with suchness.
The World-Protector proclaims the wondrous Dharma, practicing the path of the true and correct teaching;
seeing that no fixed location can be found, such is the meaning of this sutra.
Regarding all the Buddha-dharmas thus expounded, there is nothing here to be praised.
The self cannot be apprehended; how profound is this excellent exposition of the sutra!
Even if the worlds of the ten directions were naturally non-existent, that which is proclaimed by the World Protectors would not yet equal the scope of this sutra.
"Out of compassion for the world, please proclaim it; O Most Honored among Men, we pray that you expound upon it.
Recite the name of this sutra, which has not yet been mentioned.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This sutra is named 'Cūḍāmaṇi' (The Crown Jewel); you should together propagate this title.
You of great wisdom should understand why it is called 'Cūḍāmaṇi.

Just as from the summit of Mount Sumeru one can see all four continents, so too by understanding the wisdom of this sutra, one attains the four fearlessnesses and the unsurpassed Great Way, becoming free from birth, old age, sickness, and death, and crossing over the calamities of the triple world. If worldly people take delight in this Dharma, there are none throughout the ten directions who do not receive its salvation; therefore, it is called 'Cūḍāmaṇi.'"

Always uphold this; if there are those who maintain this sutra proclaimed by the Buddha, they shall act as protectors for the world and for the hundreds of billions of beings among gods and humans, giving rise to countless virtues and unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, rather than [seeking] the state of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka.

If one proclaims this Dharma, one will certainly achieve the attainment of infinite worldly protection; for having heard this Dharma that is profound and difficult to fathom, and having expounded its meaning in various places, one understands this Dharma’s deep, subtle, and unsurpassed nature, and shall thereby attain Buddhahood.
Because they are able to uphold it, they shall have no further doubt regarding any dharma.

If one receives this sutra—the supreme transformation proclaimed therein and the metaphor of the "Crown King"—one will not only attain the first stage of Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti), but shall also fully possess the three stages of patience in the second and third [stages].
That Dharma cannot be apprehended; the Way has no location and nothing to manifest as light, yet it spreads the Great Way across all phenomena.

Such a person is free from desire and seeks nothing in the present; if they uphold this sutra—the words of the King of Crowns proclaimed by the Buddha—and recite it to transform others, their merit shall be immeasurable.

If there are women who receive and uphold this sutra, they will swiftly attain excellence through the practice of wisdom. They will abandon the evil dispositions of womanhood and realize that all things are one; by knowing that the many are one, they shall uphold this Dharma, proclaim this sutra, enter into all modes of practice, and clearly understand all destinations and destinies.

By entering this Dharma, one speaks of its manifold illumination; one knows the various grades of diligent practice, and that countless beings all receive the teachings of the Way. Yet, fundamentally, there is no dharma to be proclaimed, for all things are without location and entirely unattainable.
Why is this so? Because both the beginning and the end are empty.

Since time immemorial, its meaning has been unattainable; all dharmas are thus. To uphold this gateway of the Dharma wherein no dharma can be apprehended—such that neither existence nor non-existence exists—is the inherently pure Dharma, which is then called "upholding."

Those who admire this light of immeasurable universal radiance should, at all times, expound this *Cūḍāmaṇi-rāja-sūtra*; they should extensively seek the Dharma-realm and set their will upon these eyes of light. Not perceiving any objective realm is what is called "upholding."

All dharmas are profoundly deep and unattainable; if they are unattainable, they neither exist nor do not exist. One who possesses such eloquence and sets their will upon the Buddha-way awakens in this very same manner.
To fully expound the meaning of the sutra, it is without volume and without form, like a dragon’s miraculous birth: first it raises clouds, and only then does it rain.
The mind comes from nowhere, being a synthesis of causes and conditions; this wisdom is formless and inconceivable. If one wishes to proclaim infinite dharmas, one should study this sutra.
He understands all things as empty and that there are no phenomena to which one may cling; he contemplates the scriptures without knowing their origin, and what he expounds is most excellent.
This Dharma is unarisen, as transmitted in the sutras; its light shines mysteriously like the brilliance of the sun—this light comes from nowhere and goes nowhere.
The sūtra is thus: it illuminates all that exists so that they become non-existent.

If there is a bhikṣu who maintains eloquence that is pure and uninterrupted, he should study this *Cūḍāmaṇi-rāja* with a sincere mind; through the radiance of the light of the Dharma, he will extensively propagate immeasurable truths and swiftly attain entry into unimpeded eloquence.
By studying the *Cūḍāmaṇi*, one benefits the mundane world; those who do not study this do not know the flavor of the Dharma.
There is no scripture more profound or supreme than the *Cūḍāmaṇi*; if one does not uphold it, one remains far removed from the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma.

“O assembly of bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī does not follow these scriptural precepts and instructions, nor return to their essential meaning, they will not seek that which is sought, nor attain the ultimate truth.”
If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who seek refuge in this Dharma, they act as the causal basis for all worlds; yet all dharmas are entirely beyond analogy.
It is just as if someone dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, situated within a celestial palace, could see all beneath the heavens.
One who studies this sutra universally transcends all sentient beings and delivers them all, like one standing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru and observing the world from above.
This sutra is likewise; it elucidates all phenomena and reveals that all things are non-existent, thereby guiding and transforming sentient beings.
It is just as if someone were to take a great torch and enter a dark chamber to dispel the profound gloom;
this sutra is likewise, for with the radiance of the Dharma it universally illumines all phenomena, and those who study and uphold this scripture shall never again encounter darkness.
Just as the light of the sun emerges to illuminate the world beneath heaven, reaching everywhere without exception;
so too is this sutra, which, through the radiance of the Dharma, shines upon the three realms and reveals the wisdom of the Way to all sentient beings.
Just as the lunar palace travels through the void without ceasing or resting, so too is this sutra:
it illuminates the realms of the ten directions, and all receive its grace.
This is the Dharma-seal that seals all dharmas; this seal is established for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, consider this seal: it is like empty space, entirely non-existent and incapable of being made to exist; both empty space and the seal are without expectation of one another.
The Buddha and the True Dharma are likewise so; in proclaiming this sutra, there is nothing at all that is spoken.
It is like a king who loves and honors his son, wishing to establish him as crown prince and entrust him with the kingdom's wealth.
The King said to his great ministers:
"Entrust this vast undertaking to my crown prince; furthermore, entrust this holy wealth, the kingdom, and all the myriad people to him for the future."
"The ministers obeyed the command.
Now this Dharma of the sutra is likewise so.

The youth Sudarśana received it from the Buddha and shall transmit it to countless bodhisattvas, causing them to enter the supreme Dharma; for it was the Buddha who established these essential points of the sutra’s Dharma for the sake of all bodhisattvas."

The roots of merit are blazing and vast; if one were to grasp them with the hand, their blessings would be immeasurable. One who upholds this King of Summits Sūtra as it is proclaimed therein should not harbor doubts that they will fail to attain perfect enlightenment.
If one wishes to attain eloquence regarding all phenomena without attachment, one should study this Sūtra, the Proclaimed King of Summits (Mūrdhābhiṣeka-rāja).
What is called "worldly dharma" is itself the True Path.
Why is this so? If worldly people who believe in the Way should encounter this sutra and perhaps lack faith, they will nonetheless attain the Way in the long run through the merit of having heard it.

If one receives this sutra and explains it extensively for others, all will regard them as a supreme sage; no one in the entire world can deceive them. They understand the Buddha-dharma to benefit sentient beings and serve as an unsurpassed protector of the world. If one preaches this sutra, billions of devas dwelling in the void will exclaim in praise:
“Excellent, Perfectly Awakened One!
What you have proclaimed is truly marvelous!
It is difficult to reach, exceedingly difficult to reach!”
He then expounded the sublime scriptures; these represent the excellence of the Way and the excellence of wisdom, whose benefits are inconceivable.

Whether one recites even four lines for others to explain, or diligently studies countless sutras, because this profound Dharma is inconceivable, one extensively preaches it for others. Such a person receives its grace, converses with the Buddha, and takes delight in the holy scriptures. By propagating this *Uṣṇīṣarāja* Dharma and instructing others in the essential points of the unsurpassed path of the scriptures, this is what is called "inconceivable."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If there are those who receive and uphold such a pure and sublime sūtra as this, reciting, chanting, and reading it—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—and if they are able to receive it with reverence, uphold it, and recite and read it, their merit shall be immeasurable and their achievement limitless; no one can describe its extent or find its bottom, for it is like space, whose boundaries cannot be found.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!

If one receives this sutra, even if not in great measure, but receives even a four-line verse, reciting and proclaiming it for others, the merit will be incalculable and its virtue bottomless; it is boundless and limitless, beyond all comparison.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The void may yet be measured, And all conceptual thoughts may be fully described;
But these merits and blessings Cannot be brought to their ultimate end."
To offer to the supreme world-protectors throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
if one upholds this [teaching], it is as if making offerings to all those Buddhas.
If one were to behold their various supernormal powers, they could lift up the worlds of the ten directions.
It is not as good as hearing this sutra and universally honoring all these Buddhas.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, one might abandon the tenth type of karma;
yet, even while serving the Buddhas in such a way, hearing [this sutra] is superior to making offerings.
Whether to those already passed into extinction, or to the future Buddhas,
or to the present Honored Ones among gods and men throughout the lands of the ten directions—
to all these, and to every conditioned activity, I dedicate them to the Great Benevolent Lion.
If one upholds this sūtra scroll, as proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened One,
and provides it with food and clothing, this is not the cultivation of refined wisdom;
rather, for one who upholds this practice, this is the unsurpassed offering of wisdom.

If one were to fill all the worlds of the ten directions with every kind of precious treasure and offer them to all the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the merit thereby gained would not be particularly extraordinary;
yet for one who studies this sutra proclaimed by the King of the Crown, [the merit is immeasurable].
This offering to all Buddhas is declared to be the foremost.
Regarding the sūtras I have proclaimed, one does not cling to the path of the Buddhas;
yet with a mind resting upon this, one desires to make offerings to the Tathāgatas.
Not relying on the mundane world is the foremost service;
being entirely without elevation or depreciation, this is called making offerings.
As for the Dharma of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment, nothing at all can be apprehended.
That which the Tathāgata has proclaimed is the foremost form of reverent salutation;
that which was offered and served to the Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara,
and the vision of the dharmas of all bodhisattvas, is the foremost form of making offerings.
This is the foremost offering, like serving the Buddha, the World-Honored One;
having received his prediction of enlightenment, one shall attain perfect awakening.
Desiring to abide in the Buddha-way, one becomes a perfectly awakened one, the Honored One among sentient beings.
By practicing these pure dharmas, one makes offerings to the Teacher;
through such offerings, one attains the Way that leads nowhere.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, one upholds the Dharma, and all shall proceed toward universal wisdom.
The dharmas of all Buddhas of the ten directions, as expounded by the World Protectors—all these lead toward the ultimate truth; this is the foremost offering.
Having already entered the Buddha-realm, the Buddha’s wisdom is inconceivable.
They are then able to roar the lion’s roar, just as I do today;
by means of that lion’s roar, they are courageous amidst all dharmas,
delivering and liberating billions of beings, leading them to nirvana where there is no outflow.
The Buddha again addressed Suvicintin:

“Receive this sūtra and proclaim it throughout the ten directions; let all receive, uphold, and practice the True Dharma. With boundless great wisdom, reveal it to your fellow students, enabling them to practice the six perfections and rescue those within the three realms.”
If sons or daughters of noble family receive this sutra and expound it for others, their merit will be immeasurable, just as the void cannot be measured or limited.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, the youth Subhūti, the entire assembly of noble ones, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Mahāvaipulya Śikhin-rāja Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha
